collection_summary: This instance is a curator-bounded ground truth listing 16 major Western philosophers from antiquity (Plato c. 375 BC) through the mid-20th century (Sartre 1943), each paired with a curator-selected primary canonical work (selected from the major works the philosopher's Wikipedia article identifies), the year of composition or publication of that work, and the philosophical tradition. The universe is curator-defined rather than source-list-defined because no single Wikipedia master article enumerates 'the major Western philosophers' as a clean canonical list — the philosophical canon is itself contested, and qualitative-category instances typically require curator-bounded universes when the source-canonization is fragmented. Per-row cells are source-grounded from 32 Wikipedia URLs (source_count = 32; 16 per-philosopher articles + 16 per-work articles added in cycle-1 so the Year cell is fully grounded by the cited per-work article). The 16-philosopher selection reflects philosophers commonly listed as foundational across major philosophy reference works (SEP, Routledge, Cambridge Companion to Philosophy, etc.); a v2 could expand or contract this set.
source_coverage_notes:
Roles:
- source_urls[0..15] (16 per-philosopher Wikipedia articles): entity-detail (each article lists multiple major works in the lead paragraph and 'Notable works' section, FROM WHICH the curator selects one as the staged Primary Work cell — the Wikipedia article does not designate a single 'most-canonical' work, the curator does; each article also verifies the philosopher's traditional classification — Classical Greek, Hellenistic-Roman, Medieval, Early Modern, Modern, or Contemporary)
- source_urls[16..31] (16 per-work Wikipedia articles, parallel to the philosopher articles): value (each per-work article supplies the staged Year cell — the per-work article's stated completion or publication year; for ancient/medieval works with composition windows, the latest year in the range or the conventional 'completed-by' date is used). Cycle-1 audit identified that per-philosopher articles often state composition windows or ranges rather than exact years (e.g., Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics: 'no consensus, traditional composition window 335-322 BCE'; Marcus Aurelius's Meditations: 'written between 170 and 180'); per-work articles are added to source_urls so the Year cell is fully source-grounded by a cited URL.

Multi-source Tier B instance with NO master list source. The lack of a master source-list is a deliberate design choice: no Wikipedia article cleanly enumerates 'the major Western philosophers, antiquity to mid-20th c.' as a structured wikitable. Alternative master-list candidates considered and rejected: `List of philosophers (alphabetical)` is far too broad (thousands of entries); `List of philosophical movements` is prose-only; `Western philosophy` master article is structured as historical-era prose without a single canonical philosopher-list wikitable; `Outline of Western philosophy` has multiple non-canonical lists scattered across sections. The 16-philosopher universe is therefore curator-bounded with claim_type = candidate_rebuild, signaling that the universe is a curator-curation rather than a Wikipedia master-list extraction. Per-row cells (Primary Work, Year, Tradition) ARE source-grounded from the 32-URL Wikipedia source plan (per-philosopher articles for Primary Work designation and Tradition; per-work articles for Year), so cell-level claims are source-defined even though the universe-level claim is not.
decision_log:
Candidate card (per instance_selection_priorities.md):
- Pre-gate verdict: Pass with caveats. Universe is curator-bounded (not source-defined) — flagged in claim_type=candidate_rebuild and decision_log; this is acknowledged as the inherent design constraint for qualitative-category philosophy instances. Per-row attribute cells (Primary Work, Year, Tradition) ARE source-grounded via the 32-URL Wikipedia source plan (per-philosopher articles for Primary Work designation and Tradition; per-work articles for Year, added in cycle 1). Table is LLM-knowable for a pre-2025 cutoff: very-LLM-knowable cells include canonical philosopher-text pairings (Plato/Republic, Aristotle/Nicomachean Ethics, Kant/Critique of Pure Reason, Marx/Das Kapital, Wittgenstein/Tractatus, Sartre/Being and Nothingness); mid-difficulty cells include the publication years (LLMs know within a year for modern works, within a decade for medieval, within ~50 years for antiquity); harder calibration cells include the Tradition classification at era boundaries (Marcus Aurelius 180 AD on the Hellenistic-Roman/Medieval boundary; Nietzsche 1885 vs Wittgenstein 1921 on the Modern/Contemporary boundary). Row count (16) is comfortably above the 10-row gate.
- Seed/provenance: original instance, NOT from a seed in example_questions.txt. User selected qualitative/philosophy from the gap-4 candidate slate (qualitative, geographic, comparative) — qualitative was the largest-gap tier with the most distinctive shape vs. the recent fixed-entity-list staging cluster.
- Category: qualitative (gap 4 → gap 3 after this staging) primary; temporal (gap 3) secondary because the Year column spans -375 to 1943 and provides a meaningful temporal axis. Per references/artifact-contract.md, qualitative pairs canonically with operation_type=projection (when the schema includes a text-anchored cell as one of the projected attributes); the db_analog 'SELECT philosopher, primary_work, year, tradition FROM major_western_philosophers WHERE era_overlaps(...)' is the canonical multi-column projection over a curator-bounded universe with the Primary Work column as the qualitative-anchored attribute.
- Source plan: Tier B Wikipedia, multi-source dual-URL-per-row (16 per-philosopher articles + 16 per-work articles added in cycle 1); gt_construction = manual_wikipedia; source_count = 32 (no master list).
- Expected shape: 16 rows × 4 columns; PK = Philosopher.
- Domain: Culture/Philosophy — NEW subdomain under the Culture family. Culture previously had 7 subdomains (Film, Music, Literature, Visual Arts ×2, etc.); Philosophy is the 8th subdomain. Culture family extends from 7 instances to 8.
- Risks/adaptation: (a) the universe is curator-bounded; claim_type=candidate_rebuild signals this honestly. The auditor may want the universe shrunk to a more rigorously-source-defined subset (e.g., 'philosophers listed in Wikipedia's Outline of Western philosophy main figures section') or expanded to include Eastern philosophers (Confucius, Buddha, Lao Tzu) for a non-Western-canon variant — both are documented in open_questions. (b) The 'Primary Work' cell for philosophers with multiple major works is a curator-selected single work from the source-listed set, not a Wikipedia-source-anchored designation (e.g., Plato wrote ~36 dialogues — the Plato Wikipedia article lists Republic, Phaedo, Symposium, Timaeus among major dialogues; the curator selects Republic per the 'most-anthologized' criterion). (c) The Year cell for antiquity works is curator-approximated (Plato's Republic c. 375 BC is the conventional dating; alternative datings exist in classical scholarship); the -375 staged value is the most-cited convention.
- Decision: Stage with claim_type=candidate_rebuild flag for the universe-curation acknowledgment.

Why original rather than seed-driven: no seed in example_questions.txt targets `qualitative` directly (qualitative is structurally the hardest category to seed because it's text/concept-anchored rather than entity-attribute-anchored).

Why this shape (Western philosophers × primary work × year × tradition) rather than alternatives discussed in the next-pick conversation: variant-qualitative-philosophy was chosen over geographic/deserts and comparative/dual-Olympics because (a) `qualitative` is structurally the most distinctive of the 3 remaining gap-4 categories (text-anchored vs. the numeric/temporal/categorical shapes that dominate the rest of the benchmark); (b) the philosopher-text pairing is a canonical qualitative-knowledge axis that the benchmark hasn't tested; (c) Culture/Philosophy is a NEW subdomain (Culture currently at 7 subdomains); (d) the calibration gradient is rich (canonical author-work pairings are easy; era boundaries and approximate dates are harder).

Why curator-bounded universe (claim_type=candidate_rebuild) rather than source-defined: no Wikipedia master article enumerates 'major Western philosophers' as a clean source-list. Attempts to find such a list: (a) `List of philosophers (alphabetical)` — too broad, thousands of entries; (b) `List of philosophical movements` — prose-only; (c) `Western philosophy` main article — prose-organized by historical era without a canonical philosopher-list wikitable; (d) `Outline of Western philosophy` — has multiple non-canonical lists scattered across sections. The 16-philosopher curator-bounded universe is the alternative; claim_type=candidate_rebuild honestly signals this. The auditor may push back on universe rigor; if so, options include (i) narrowing to a single-era subset like 'Hellenistic philosophers with surviving works' (clean Wikipedia source but row count below gate) or 'Continental philosophers 20th century' (~10-15 figures with clean Wikipedia source); (ii) widening to include Eastern philosophical figures (Confucius, Buddha, Lao Tzu, Nāgārjuna, etc.) with claim_type still candidate_rebuild; (iii) pivoting to a completely different qualitative shape like 'major scientific revolutions × landmark publication' or 'world religions × canonical scripture'.

Category ↔ operation_type pairing: qualitative pairs reasonably with operation_type=projection per references/artifact-contract.md. The 3-attribute SELECT per row (Primary Work, Year, Tradition) over the curator-bounded universe is the canonical qualitative-category structure when the qualitative test is on the Primary Work designation (recall the canonical text most closely associated with each philosopher).

Domain selection: Culture/Philosophy — first instance in the Philosophy subdomain. Culture family now has 7 → 8 subdomains. Philosophy is a natural fit because the Primary Work designations are humanities texts; alternative classification under History/Philosophy would be defensible (philosophy IS historically situated) but the Culture/Philosophy subdomain is more conventional for the philosophy-as-canonical-text framing.

Post-audit (2026-05-12, cycle 1): the cycle-1 audit raised 2 BLOCKING + 2 NON-BLOCKING HYGIENE + 1 SUGGESTION. (a) BLOCKING #1 — Year cells not source-grounded by the cited per-philosopher URLs: the cycle-0 source_urls listed only 16 per-philosopher Wikipedia articles, but several Year values came from per-work articles that the source_urls didn't include. Per-philosopher articles often state composition windows or ranges ('no consensus, 335-322 BCE'; 'written between 170 and 180') rather than exact years, making the staged integer Year cells not fully grounded by the cited URLs. (b) BLOCKING #2 — Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics Year = -340 was unsupported: the Aristotle Wikipedia page labels Nicomachean Ethics as c. 322 BC, and the per-work article gives the traditional composition window as 335-322 BCE — neither source supports the cycle-0 staged value of -340. Also flagged: Marcus Aurelius's Meditations Year = 175 was inside the 170-180 AD window but not exactly source-supported. Both BLOCKINGs resolved by: (1) adding 16 per-work Wikipedia article URLs to source_urls (source_count 16 → 32; per-work articles are the canonical source for exact Year cells); (2) updating Aristotle Year -340 → -322 (per Nicomachean Ethics article's 335-322 BCE composition window, taking the latest year per the conventional 'completed-by' convention for works with composition windows); (3) updating Marcus Aurelius Year 175 → 180 (per his Wikipedia article's 170-180 AD range, taking his death year 180 as the conventional 'completed-by' date for posthumously-compiled works). For consistency, all 16 Year cells now use the 'completed-by / latest year in range / publication year' convention as documented in normalization_decisions. Net cycle-1 changes: 2 CSV Year cell repairs (Aristotle -340→-322, Marcus Aurelius 175→180); 16 new per-work URLs added to source_urls (source_count 16→32); narrative updates in temporal_note and source_coverage_notes for the dual-URL-per-row sourcing pattern.

Post-audit (2026-05-12, cycle 2): the cycle-2 audit returned Ready with 0 BLOCKING + 2 NON-BLOCKING HYGIENE + 1 SUGGESTION. (a) HYGIENE #1 — stale 'old 16-source pattern' references: cycle-1 fix updated source_count and source_urls but left several narrative fields still claiming '16 per-philosopher Wikipedia articles' or 'source_count = 16'. Resolved by sweeping all stale '16 per-philosopher only' references to the new '32-URL (16 per-philosopher + 16 per-work added in cycle 1)' framing across temporal_note, _extraction_notes, collection_summary, source_coverage_notes, decision_log Pre-gate / Source-plan bullets. (b) HYGIENE #2 — stale Aristotle/Marcus Year examples (-340, 175 AD) appearing in narrative-example contexts that survived cycle-1: the calibration-cell paragraph mentioned 'Marcus Aurelius 175 AD' as the Hellenistic-Roman/Medieval boundary example; the Year normalization paragraph mentioned 'Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics c. 340 BC = -340'; the Era-boundary case explanation said 'Marcus Aurelius (175 AD) is classified Hellenistic-Roman'. Resolved by updating all three to 180 AD / -322 to match the cycle-1-corrected CSV values. (c) SUGGESTION — Primary Work provenance wording should be softened to reflect curator selection among source-listed major works: the cycle-0/1 Primary Work normalization paragraph said the cell is 'the most-cited canonical work per the philosopher's Wikipedia article', which overstates the Wikipedia-source-anchoring (Wikipedia articles often list multiple major works without designating ONE as 'the most-cited canonical'). Resolved by softening to 'a curator-selected single work from the set of major works the philosopher's Wikipedia article identifies' with the curator's per-row selection rationale documented (Plato Republic over Phaedo/Symposium/etc.; Aristotle Nicomachean Ethics over Politics/Metaphysics/etc.; Hume Treatise over Enquiry; Marx Das Kapital over Communist Manifesto). The 'curator-selected' framing is more honest than 'most-canonical' because canonization is itself contested in philosophical reference contexts. Net cycle-2 changes: 0 CSV changes; 0 source_urls changes; multi-location narrative cleanup across draft.json _extraction_notes and curation.json collection_summary / source_coverage_notes / decision_log / normalization_decisions to clear residual stale phrases and soften Primary Work provenance wording.

Post-audit (2026-05-12, cycle 3 verification): the cycle-3 verification audit returned Ready with 0 BLOCKING + 2 NON-BLOCKING HYGIENE + 0 SUGGESTION. The cycle-2 fixes were mostly clean but two residual HYGIENE items survived: (a) open_questions item 4 still used '175 CE' as the BCE/CE marker example (cycle-2 fix updated calibration/Year-normalization/Era-boundary references to 180 but missed this one); resolved by updating to '180 CE'. (b) Primary Work provenance wording outside the cycle-2-fixed normalization_decisions paragraph still implied Wikipedia source-anchors the single-work designation — specifically: temporal_note said 'The Primary Work designation reflects each philosopher's most-cited and most-anthologized text per their per-philosopher Wikipedia article' (overstates source-anchoring); _extraction_notes step (3) said 'Primary Work designation taken from the article's lead paragraph or Notable works section, selecting the most-canonical title where multiple major works exist' (overstates source-anchoring); source_coverage_notes per-philosopher-URL role said 'each article supplies the philosopher's Primary Work designation' (implies the Wikipedia article designates, when actually it lists multiple works that the curator selects from); decision_log Risks/adaptation bullet (b) said 'Republic is the conventional choice' (implies a Wikipedia-source convention exists when actually it's curator selection). All four resolved by reframing to 'curator selects one of the source-listed major works per the most-anthologized-in-undergraduate-reference criterion' across all four narrative locations. Net cycle-3 changes: 0 CSV; 0 source_urls; 5 narrative cleanups (open_questions BCE/CE example + 4 Primary Work provenance phrasings in temporal_note, _extraction_notes, source_coverage_notes, decision_log Risks bullet).
normalization_decisions: Universe definition: the staged universe is a curator-bounded set of 16 major Western philosophers from antiquity (Plato c. 375 BC) through the mid-20th century (Sartre 1943). The curator-bounding criteria are: (a) each philosopher is universally listed as foundational across major philosophy reference works (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Routledge Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Cambridge Companion to Philosophy, etc.); (b) each has a dedicated Wikipedia article; (c) each has a single most-cited primary work that the Wikipedia article identifies in the lead paragraph or 'Notable works' section; (d) the set spans 6 traditions for tradition-axis calibration. The 16-philosopher selection is curator-defined rather than source-list-defined; claim_type=candidate_rebuild acknowledges this. Excluded by the curator-bounding rule: pre-Socratic philosophers (Thales, Heraclitus, Parmenides — surviving works are fragmentary, no clear single 'primary work'); minor Hellenistic philosophers (Epicurus, Zeno of Citium, Pyrrho — surviving works are fragmentary); contemporary post-1945 philosophers (Foucault, Derrida, Habermas, Rawls — multiple major works without a single canonical choice; era boundary at WWII end). Excluded by scope: Eastern philosophers (Confucius, Buddha, Lao Tzu, Nāgārjuna — outside Western tradition scope; could be added as a v2 'Major philosophers across traditions' instance). Philosopher name normalization: each philosopher's name is the conventional English short-form per their Wikipedia article — 'Aquinas' (not 'Thomas Aquinas' or 'St. Thomas Aquinas'); 'Marcus Aurelius' (full name because 'Aurelius' alone is ambiguous); 'Descartes' (single name, conventional); 'Hegel' (single name); 'Kant' (single name); 'Marx' / 'Nietzsche' / 'Wittgenstein' / 'Heidegger' / 'Sartre' (single name). For philosophers conventionally referenced by full first+last name in academic prose, the Wikipedia article title's short-form is used. Primary Work normalization: the staged Primary Work cell is a **curator-selected single work** from the set of major works the philosopher's Wikipedia article identifies. The selection criterion is 'the most-anthologized and most-cited work in undergraduate-philosophy reference contexts'; this is curator judgment, not a Wikipedia-source-defined designation. Where multiple major works exist on a philosopher's Wikipedia article, the curator's choice is documented per-row: (a) for Plato — Republic chosen (the philosopher's Wikipedia article also lists Apology, Phaedo, Symposium, Timaeus among major dialogues); (b) for Aristotle — Nicomachean Ethics chosen (the philosopher's Wikipedia article also lists Politics, Metaphysics, Physics, De Anima); (c) for Hume — A Treatise of Human Nature chosen (the philosopher's Wikipedia article also lists An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding); (d) for Marx — Das Kapital chosen (the philosopher's Wikipedia article also lists The Communist Manifesto co-authored with Engels and Economic and Philosophical Manuscripts of 1844). The 'curator-selected' framing is more honest than 'most-canonical' because canonization is itself contested (e.g., a scholar focused on political philosophy might pick Aristotle's Politics over Nicomachean Ethics; the curator's selection reflects general-reference-text conventions). Year normalization: integer year of composition or publication, with BC dates rendered as negative integers. The 'completed-by / latest year in range / publication year' convention is applied uniformly: (a) Plato Republic c. 375 BC = -375 (per-work article's most-cited convention); (b) Aristotle Nicomachean Ethics = -322 per the per-work article's 335-322 BCE composition window (latest year, Aristotle's death year); (c) Marcus Aurelius Meditations = 180 per the 170-180 AD range (Marcus Aurelius's death year, conventional 'completed-by' for posthumously-compiled work); (d) Augustine City of God = 426 (completion, per per-work article); (e) Aquinas Summa Theologica = 1274 (Aquinas's death year, unfinished at his death, conventional 'completed-by' date). For modern works (post-1500), the publication year is verbatim from the work's first edition (Machiavelli's Prince 1532; Descartes's Meditations 1641; Locke's Essay 1689; etc.). For Hume's Treatise, the publication year is 1739 (Book I and II; Book III followed in 1740 — staged value uses 1739 as the first-publication year). For Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra, the publication year is 1885 (final completion; serialized 1883-1885 — staged value uses 1885 as the completed-work date). Tradition normalization: 6-value categorical (Classical Greek, Hellenistic-Roman, Medieval, Early Modern, Modern, Contemporary). Era boundaries are: Classical Greek = pre-Socratic + Plato/Aristotle (4th-c. BC); Hellenistic-Roman = post-Aristotle Greek + Roman (3rd c. BC – 5th c. AD; Marcus Aurelius 180 AD falls here); Medieval = 5th-15th c. AD (Augustine 426, Aquinas 1274); Early Modern = 16th-18th c. (Machiavelli 1532, Descartes 1641, Locke 1689, Hume 1739); Modern = late 18th-19th c. (Kant 1781, Hegel 1807, Marx 1867, Nietzsche 1885); Contemporary = 20th c. (Wittgenstein 1921, Heidegger 1927, Sartre 1943). Era-boundary cases: Marcus Aurelius (180 AD) is classified Hellenistic-Roman (not Medieval, which begins with the Western Roman Empire's fall c. 476 AD). Augustine (426) is classified Medieval (he is the patristic-medieval transition figure). The 'Contemporary' category stops at 1945 (Sartre's Being and Nothingness 1943) — post-WWII philosophers are excluded by the universe-bounding rule. Alphabetical sort: the CSV is sorted alphabetically by Philosopher name (Aquinas, Aristotle, Augustine, ..., Sartre, Wittgenstein), matching the standard convention for fixed-entity-list instances.
open_questions: 1. Whether the universe should be narrowed to a more rigorously source-defined subset. Options: (a) 'Hellenistic philosophers with surviving works' — clean Wikipedia source but row count below gate; (b) 'Continental philosophers, 20th century' — Wikipedia 'Continental philosophy' article has a clean main-figures section; (c) 'Founders of major philosophical schools listed in Wikipedia's Hellenistic philosophy article' — 4-6 schools, too narrow. The current curator-bounded universe is the broadest defensible choice but trades off source-rigor. 2. Whether the universe should be widened to include Eastern philosophers (Confucius, Buddha, Lao Tzu, Nāgārjuna, Śaṅkara, etc.) for a 'Major philosophers across traditions' instance. The current Western-only scope is curator-bounded; a v2 with cross-tradition inclusion would yield ~25 rows but introduces tradition-classification complexity (e.g., is Confucius's Analects a philosophical text or a religious-cultural one?). 3. Whether 'Primary Work' should be a curator-selected most-canonical work or a comprehensive list of all major works. The current single-work staging is the cleanest qualitative-test shape (test the LLM's ability to identify THE canonical work per philosopher); a multi-work variant would be a multi-attribute_projection rather than qualitative shape. 4. Whether the Year cell should include BCE/CE markers ('375 BCE', '180 CE') rather than negative-integer (-375) and positive-integer (180). The current numeric representation is cleaner for SQL queries but loses the BCE/CE annotation; a v2 could add an Era marker column. 5. Whether the Tradition classification should be more granular (e.g., split 'Modern' into 'Romanticism vs Analytic precursors'; split 'Contemporary' into 'Analytic / Continental / Existentialist'). The current 6-value categorical balances granularity vs. row count (6 categories across 16 rows = ~2-3 per category on average). 6. Whether to add post-WWII philosophers (Foucault, Derrida, Habermas, Rawls, Kuhn, etc.) for a more contemporary-inclusive instance. The current mid-20th-c. cutoff excludes them; a v2 extension to 1980-1990s would add 5-10 more rows but with weaker single-canonical-work attribution (most contemporary philosophers wrote multiple major works without a clearly-dominant primary). 7. Whether the universe selection criteria should be made more explicit and Wikipedia-anchorable. The current 'universally listed as foundational across major philosophy reference works' is curator-defined; a Wikipedia-anchored alternative would be 'philosophers whose Wikipedia article includes the {{Philosophy}} infobox AND a 'Major works' section with at least one work cited in 100+ academic books per Google Scholar metric' — but this requires per-article infobox + Scholar metric verification.
